Similarly to the Katori descendant deities mentioned above, at Kashima Jingū the Kashima descendant deities are also spread throughout Mutsu Province – eight shrines in total are recorded in the ''Engishiki Jinmyōchō''. This has led scholars to believe that when the Yamato court expanded northward along the coast, it invoked the divine power of both the Kashima and Katori deities{{Sfn|鹿島御児神社（国史）|1983}}. In addition, at {{ill|Shiogama shrine|en|Shiogama shrine|qid=Q133753|lt=Shiogama shrine|1=Shiogama shrine}}—the Ichinomiya of Mutsu (located in Shiogama City, Miyagi Prefecture, {{Coord|38|19|08.12|N|141|00|45.47|E|region:JP-04_type:landmark|name=Ichinomiya of Mutsu: Shiogama Shrine (enshrining Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi together)}})—the deities Takemikazuchi and Futsunushi are enshrined together, which further exemplifies this phenomenon{{Sfn|鹿島御児神社（国史）|1983}}.

It is said that in the initial stages Kashima was oriented toward the open sea (Ezo) while Katori was oriented toward the inner sea (the Katori Sea){{Sfn|香取神宮（神々）|1984}}. Later, although only two of the above Katori descendant deities remained, both came to be enshrined in Kurihara District (in the present-day area around Kurihara City, Miyagi Prefecture), effectively bypassing Kashima—which has its northernmost presence in Oshika District (around present-day Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture)—and being established further north{{Sfn|香取神宮（神々）|1984}}. In this connection, scholars point to factors such as the likelihood that governance of Kurihara District became possible by the 9th century, that from 811 (Kōnin 3) the Mononobe Sōsaji clan (a clan associated with Sōsaji District in Kazusa Province) appears as the general of the Mutsu Provincial Administration, and that in 839 (Shōwa 6) the divine Rank of the Katori deity caught up with that of the Kashima deity; in addition, the record lists the names in the order “Katori, Kashima,” suggesting that the divine authority of the Kashima and Katori deities may have been reversed as a result of the activities of the Mononobe Sōsaji clan{{Sfn|香取神宮（神々）|1984}}.

Furthermore, in the low-lying, marshy areas along the Tone and Edo Rivers in the western part of the former Kazusa Province, as these areas were developed from the 10th century onward, the Katori deity was enshrined as a local tutelary deity – which explains the widespread distribution of many branch shrines (see [[Katori Jingu|Katori Shrine]]){{Sfn|香取小史|1995|p=40}}. Additionally, a connection has been noted with [[Ichinomiya Nukina Shrine]]—the Ichinomiya of Ueno Province (located in Tomioka City, Gunma Prefecture), which also enshrines Futsunushi{{Sfn|香取小史|1995|p=41}}.

=== Katori Jingū-ji ===
In the past, Katori Jingu had three temples functioning as its jingu-ji (temple annexes): Kongō Hōji (now defunct), Tōkōzan Sōjiin, and Shinfukuji{{Sfn|香取神宮（平凡社）|1996}}. Kongō Hōji, located on Miyachūdai, served as the Bettō-ji (assigned temple) of the shrine{{Sfn|香取神宮（平凡社）|1996}}. Tōkōzan Sōjiin was known as a temple for the serving monks and belonged to the Shingon sect (Chizankai branch){{Sfn|香取神宮（平凡社）|1996}}. Shinfukuji, known by the mountain name Keitsu Jintoku-san, belonged to the Sōtō sect (now part of the Rinzai sect – Myōshin-ji branch){{Sfn|香取神宮（平凡社）|1996}}, and in the early modern period it possessed an income equivalent to 34 koku of rice{{Sfn|香取神宮（角川）|1984}}. Of these, Kongō Hōji became defunct in the early Meiji period{{Sfn|香取神宮（平凡社）|1996}}, and Sōjiin was relocated from Oino to Sawara.

== Critical Examination ==
=== Regarding the Enshrined Deities and the Worshipping Clans ===
One theory regarding the founding of the shrine holds that the Yamato court established the enshrinement of both deities as a base for its eastern expansion, and that this act constituted the origin of the worship at the shrine<ref name="香取遺産"/>{{Sfn|香取神宮（平凡社）|1996}}; other theories propose that a more primordial form of worship existed even before that (see below).

Furthermore, although the current Katori Jingu officially names its principal deity as [[Futsunushi|Futsunushi]] (Keitsushu), according to the ''Nihon Shoki'' Futsunushi is also known by the alternate name “Ihahinushi” (Iwahinushi/Saishu). In documents discussing its relationship with the shrine, the ''Shoku Nihongi'', ''Nihon Buntokuten Tennō Jitsuroku'', and ''Engishiki'' use the name Ihahinushi, while the ''Kogo Shūi'' employs Futsunushi. From these divine names, the following debates concerning the early period of the shrine have emerged.

'''Futsunushi (Keitsushu)'''
: The term “Futsu” is said to express the sharpness of a sword and is thus regarded as a divine name representing swords{{Sfn|香取神宮（国史）|1983}}.
: In connection with this, the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki mention a divine sword called [[Futsunomitama]] (Futsunomitama, also rendered as Futsunoritama), which was bestowed from Takemikazuchi to Takakurashita and later enshrined at Ishigami Shrine (in Tenri City, Nara Prefecture) as the tutelary deity of the Mononobe clan.
: The divine names Futsunushi and [[Waka-Futsunushi]] also appear frequently in the ''Izumo Fudoki'' and are said to be distributed across many regions<ref name="松前">[[Matsumae Ken]] ''A Book That Illuminates the Mysteries of Japanese Mythology'', Yamato Shobō, 2007, pp. 126–129.</ref>. This is thought to be because the Mononobe clan, after having venerated the divine sword Futsunomitama in their campaigns, deified it as Futsunushi in various regions<ref name="松前"/>.
: Based on these traditions, Futsunushi is explained as appearing in the land‐transfer myth<ref name="松前"/>.
: On the other hand, since Futsunushi does not appear in the Kojiki, there is a theory that it was derived from the alternative name “Tatefutsu/Toyofutsu” for Takemikazuchi that does appear in the Kojiki<ref>『国史大辞典』, Entry: Keitsushu.</ref>.

'''Ihahinushi (Iwai-nushi, Iwahinushi/Saishu)'''
: From the meaning of the characters for “iwau” (which can be read as “sai” or “shuku” meaning “to perform a ritual” or “celebrate”), the name Ihahinushi is conjectured to mean “the executor of rituals”{{Sfn|岡田|2011}}.
: Proponents of interpreting the Katori deity as Ihahinushi argue that all texts except the ''Kogo Shūi'' record the name as Ihahinushi, which is taken as evidence{{Sfn|岡田|2011}}.
: Regarding the fact that only the ''Kogo Shūi'' gives a different account, one theory suggests that Saibe Hiroshige did not possess accurate knowledge about the Nakatomi deity{{Sfn|岡田|2011}}.
: Moreover, the divine names suggest a structure analogous to that of Ise Jingu’s inner and outer shrines – with “Kashima” as the court deity and “Katori” as the local, serving deity –{{Sfn|香取神宮（神々）|1984}}{{Sfn|岡田|2011}}{{Sfn|千葉県の歴史 通史編 古代2|2001|pp=613–628}}.
: In addition, the fact that the divine Rank (shinkai) of the Katori deity lags behind that of Kashima and that it does not receive honors is also thought to be due to its role as a serving deity; furthermore, since enshrinement was traditionally a female responsibility, some have argued that the enshrined deity should be regarded as a goddess{{Sfn|香取神宮（神々）|1984}}.

As for the worshipping clans, it is known that the Katori clan (Katōri-uji) originally claimed descent from the deity of Keitsushu; however, there is a theory that the essence of the Katori clan is actually that of the Mononobe clan{{Sfn|香取神宮（神々）|1984}}. In this context, based on the relationship between Futsunomitama and Futsunushi and the presence of Mononobe clans in historical records, it is conjectured that Futsunushi was enshrined as the tutelary deity of the Mononobe clan{{Sfn|香取神宮（神々）|1984}}{{Sfn|千葉県の歴史 通史編 古代2|2001|pp=613–628}}. On the other hand, there is also a theory that Katori Jingu was the tutelary shrine of the Shimokamijukuni, and that the Tada Hifumbei clan (おさだのひまつりべうじ), which held that office, represents the original clan{{Sfn|岡田|2011}}. The Tada Hifumbei were a religiously oriented group of bumins with a Kabane called Atai that emphasized subordination, a characteristic seen as consistent with the serving nature implied by the name Ihahinushi{{Sfn|岡田|2011}}. Conversely, some scholars view the Katori clan as having been under the control of this Shimokamijukuni lineage{{Sfn|松尾|2014|pp=260–265}}.

=== Nearby Kofun (Ancient Tombs) ===
[[File:Matami-kofun sekishitsu.JPG|thumb|180px|right|{{Center|Matami Kofun}}]]
[[File:Shintoyama-kofun.JPG|thumb|190px|right|{{Center|Zenpō-kōen-fun of the Shintoyama Kofun Group}}]]
Several ancient tombs have been discovered in the vicinity of the shrine:
* Matami Kofun (a designated historic site of Katori City)
: This is the ancient tomb that remains closest to the shrine. At the grounds of Matami Shrine (an external subsidiary shrine), a horizontal cave-style stone chamber is exposed, although the tumulus itself no longer survives. It is dated to the mid-7th century<ref>[http://www.city.katori.lg.jp/05sightseeing/kyouiku/bunkazai/b05c.html#Vol-029 Vol-029 Matami Kofun] (Katori City “Katori Heritage” website)</ref>.
* Shintoyama Kofun Group (a designated historic site of Katori City)
: This group of tombs, located to the north of the shrine, consists of one zenpō-kōen-fun and 11 circular tombs, and is dated to around the 6th century<ref name="神道山">[http://www.city.katori.lg.jp/05sightseeing/kyouiku/bunkazai/b05d.html#Vol-039 Vol-039 Shintoyama Kofun Group] (Katori City “Katori Heritage” website)</ref>. Among these, the zenpō-kōen-fun has a total length of 46.8 meters; when it was first discovered in Showa 3 (1928), there was debate that it might have been the mausoleum of the deity Keitsushu<ref name="神道山"/>.
* Tsumiya Kofun Group
: This group, located in the northeastern part of Shintoyama, comprises three zenpō-kōen-fun and one circular tomb<ref name="ふさ"/>.
Although a relationship between these ancient tombs and the shrine has been suggested, no written records or traditions concerning these tombs have been preserved by the shrine, and the details remain unclear.

Furthermore, in Komigawa in Katori City, which lies somewhat to the east, there are many large ancient tombs – including the Sannobunme Ōtsukayama Kofun (a zenpō-kōen-fun measuring 123 meters) dating from the mid-5th century and Jōyama No. 1 Kofun (a zenpō-kōen-fun measuring 68 meters) dating from the mid-6th century<ref>[http://www.city.katori.lg.jp/05sightseeing/kyouiku/bunkazai/b05c.html#Vol-034 Vol-034 Jōyama No. 1 Kofun] (Katori City “Katori Heritage” website)</ref> – which are considered to have been the strongholds of the Shimokamijukuni.

== Local Information ==
'''Location'''
* 1697 Katori, [[Katori City]], {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|en|Chiba Prefecture|qid=Q80011|lt=Chiba Prefecture|1=Chiba Prefecture}}
'''Facilities'''
* Treasure Hall – Open from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM. Exhibits include treasures such as the Sea Mammal Grapevine Mirror (a National Treasure) and others.

'''Access'''
* Rail
** {{ill|Katori Station|en|Katori Station|qid=Q6377809|lt=Katori Station|1=Katori Station}} – Served by JR East (Narita Line and Kashima Line)
*** Approximately 30 minutes on foot via the Tsumiya Approach
*** A shuttle bus operates during the first three days of the New Year
** {{ill|Sawara Station|en|Sawara Station|qid=Q5359841|lt=Sawara Station|1=Sawara Station}} – on the JR East Narita Line
*** Approximately 50 minutes on foot via the Omotesandō
*** About 10 minutes by taxi
*** Approximately 20 minutes by rental bicycle (available at Sawara Station and other locations)
* Bus
** [[Chiba Kōtsū]] Bus, Kamisato Line – Operates daily
** [[Katori City Circulation Bus]]
*** Ōto/Mizuho Route – Weekdays only
*** Loop Route – There are different routes for weekdays and for weekends/holidays (operating on Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays)
* Highway Bus
** {{ill|Keisei Bus|en|Keisei Bus|qid=Q11374367|lt=Keisei Bus|1=Keisei Bus}} and [[Chiba Kōtsū]] Tone Liner (routes: Sawara Route, Komigawa–Sawara Route, Komigawa Route)
**: Departs from in front of the Yaesu Exit of {{ill|Tokyo Station|en|Tokyo Station|qid=Q283196|lt=Tokyo Station|1=Tokyo Station}} (next to the Tokyo Tatemono Building) and passes through Daiei Bus Stop.
*** Sawara Route: Get off at the “Sawara Station North Exit” and “In Front of Katori City Hall” stops.
*** Komigawa–Sawara Route: Get off at “Sawara Station North Exit”, “In Front of Katori City Hall”, and “Sawara–Katori (【[[:File:佐原香取インターチェンジ|Sawara–Katori IC]}])” stops.
*** Komigawa Route: Get off at “Sawara–Katori (Sawara–Katori IC)” stop.
** {{ill|Kantō Railway|en|Kantō Railway|qid=Q845943|lt=Kantō Railway|1=Kantō Railway}} – Asō-go (departing from {{ill|Tokyo Station|en|Tokyo Station|qid=Q283196|lt=Tokyo Station|1=Tokyo Station}})
*** Get off at the “Katori Jingu” bus stop.
* By Car
** Approximately 1 km from the [[Sawara–Katori Interchange]] on the {{ill|Higashi-Kantō Expressway|en|Higashi-Kantō Expressway|qid=Q864875|lt=Higashi-Kantō Expressway|1=Higashi-Kantō Expressway}}
** Parking: Free parking (approximately 400 spaces) and private paid parking

'''Surroundings'''
* The historic streetscape of {{ill|Sawara|en|Sawara|qid=Q1417327|lt=Sawara|1=Sawara}}
** [[Ino Tadataka Memorial Museum]]
* [[Suigo Sawara Yama Kuruma Kaikan]]
* [[Suigo Sawara Ayame Park]] – Located across the Tone River
* [[Kankokuji (Makino, Katori City)|Kankokuji]] (in Makino, Katori City) – Conveys the four hanging Buddhist statues associated with Katori Jingu (an Important Cultural Property)<ref>[http://www.city.katori.lg.jp/05sightseeing/kyouiku/bunkazai/b05f.html#Vol-052 Vol-052 The Masterpiece of Hanging Buddhist Statues] (Katori City “Katori Heritage” website)</ref>

[[Image:Katori-jinngu-shrine-torii,katori-city,japan.JPG|thumb|right|220px|{{Center|Second Torii}}]]'''Katori Shrine'' (Katori Jingu) is a {{ill|lt=Shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945|1=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|lt=Chiba Prefecture|Q80011|qid=Q80011|1=Chiba Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Katori City|Q858357|qid=Q858357|1=Katori, Chiba}} Katori. {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinai Shrine|1=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}}), {{ill|lt=Shimosa Province|Q1053695|qid=Q1053695|1=Shimōsa Province}}{{ill|lt=Ichinomiya|Q1656379|qid=Q1656379|1=Ichinomiya}}. {{ill|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System|Q712534|comment=this used to link to modern system but that one is too overlinked|lt=Old Shrine Ranking|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}} is {{ill|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System|Q712534|comment=this used to link to modern system but that one is too overlinked|lt=Old Shrine Ranking|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}} is {{ill|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System#Government Shrine|Q712534|comment=this used to link to modern system but that one is too overlinked|lt=Kanpei Taisha|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}, and currently it is {{ill|lt=Beppyō Shrine|Q10898274|qid=Q10898274|1=Beppyo shrine}} of {{ill|lt=Shrine Head Office|Q908077|qid=Q908077|1=Association of Shinto Shrines}}.

The main headquarters of {{ill|lt=Katori Shrine|Q11667187|qid=Q11667187|1=Katori Shrines}}, of which there are approximately 400 companies nationwide, mainly in the Kanto region|Q132480}}. {{ill|lt=Kashima Shrine|Q706499|qid=Q706499|1=Kashima Jingū}} in {{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|qid=Q83273|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Kashima City|Q467471|qid=Q467471|1=Kashima, Ibaraki}}, {{ill|lt=Kashima Shrine|Q706499|qid=Q706499|1=Kashima Jingū}} in Ibaraki Prefecture {{ill|lt=Kamisu City|Q840595|qid=Q840595|1=Kamisu}} Along with {jalink|Ikusu Shrine|Q11073095}}, it is one of the {{ill|lt=Togokusansha|Q17222093|qid=Q17222093|1=Tōgoku Sansha}}<ref>[http://www.kamisu-kanko.jp/power/ Togoku Sansha] (Kamisu City Tourism Association). </ref>. It is also a shrine that is worshiped from a distance in the {{ill|lt=four directions|Q11419901|qid=Q11419901|1=Shihohai}} of the imperial court. 

=== Overview ===
It is located on a hill called "Kamegaseyama" on the right bank downstream of {{ill|lt=Tone River|Q177452|qid=Q177452|1=Tone River}} in the northeastern part of {{ill|lt=Chiba Prefecture|Q80011|qid=Q80011|1=Chiba Prefecture}}. It is one of the oldest shrines in the country, known for enshrining {{ill|lt=Kyotsu no Nushikami|Q1107286|qid=Q1107286|1=Futsunushi}} (Futunushi), who played an active role in {{ill|lt=Japanese Mythology|Q814158|qid=Q814158|1=Japanese mythology}}, who played an active role at the time of the ceding of the land of the Ōkuninushi in {{ill|lt=Japanese mythology|Q814158|qid=Q814158|1=Japanese mythology}}.

In ancient times, it was revered by the Imperial Court as the Heidai deity for {{ill|lt=Ezo|Q932574|qid=Q932574|1=Emishi}}, and by the {{ill|lt=Fujiwara clan|Q641628|qid=Q641628|1=Fujiwara clan}} as one of the {{ill|lt=guardian deities|Q767655|qid=Q767655|1=Ujigami}}. Its divine power continued from the {{ill|lt=medieval period|Q12554|qid=Q12554|1=Middle Ages}} to the {{ill|lt=samurai|Q2927809|qid=Q2927809|1=Buke}} era, and was revered as {{ill|lt=God of War|Q11124822|qid=Q11124822|1=武神}} by successive samurai governments. Even today, it is a shrine that is deeply worshiped by those in the {{ill|lt=martial arts|Q752021|qid=Q752021|1=Budō}} field.As a cultural property, the {{ill|lt=Sea Beast Grape Mirror|Q11151137|qid=Q11151137|1=Sea-beast grape mirror}} from the {{ill|lt=Tang Dynasty|Q9683|qid=Q9683|1=Tang dynasty}} dynasty has been designated as a {{ill|lt=National Treasure|Q1139795|qid=Q1139795|1=National Treasure (Japan)}}. In terms of buildings, {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963|1=Edo period}} {{ill|lt=main shrine|Q2044994|qid=Q2044994|1=Honden}}, {{ill|lt=romon|Q97378762|qid=Q97378762|1=Rōmon}}, art Among the crafts, the mirror from the Heian period and the old Seto guardian dogs from the Middle Ages have been designated as national important cultural properties, and many other cultural properties have been handed down to the present day.

=== Enshrined God ===
The following deity is enshrined:<ref group="Note">The description that there is one deity enshrined is based on official descriptions in [http://www.katori-jingu.or.jp/goyuisyo.htm Goyūsho] (official website), ``Shinshu Katori Jingu Short History,'' shrine history book, etc. However, {{ill|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi no Mikoto|1=Takemikazuchi}} (Takemikazuchi no Mikoto), {{j alink|Amagiya-no-Mikoto|Q2564508|Amenokoyane-no-Mikoto}} (Amenokoyane no Mikoto) and {{ill|lt=Hime-kami|Q22070227|qid=Q22070227|1=Himegami}} (Himegami) are listed in some documents. </ref>.

* '''{{ill|lt=Ketsunushi no Okami|Q1107286|qid=Q1107286|lt=Ketsunushi no Okami|1=Futsunushi}}''' (Futsunushi wolf)
*: Other names are '''Ihabisu-kami''/'''Sainushi-no-kami'' and '''Saino-adult'' (Ihahi-no-ushi).

=== About the enshrined deity ===
As mentioned above, the main deity enshrined at Katori Shrine is known as {{ill|lt=Ketsunushi|Q1107286|qid=Q1107286|lt=Futunushi|1=Futsunushi}} (Ketsunushi). Regarding its origin, "{{ill|lt=Nihon Shoki|Q813935|qid=Q813935|1=Nihon Shoki}}" ({{ill|lt=720 years|Q23539|qid=Q23539|1=720}}) states that it is a different legend. </ref>, It is said that when {{ill|lt=Izanagi|Q813858|qid=Q813858|1=Izanagi}} (Izanagi Takashi) cut {{ill|lt=Kagutsuchi|Q1640658|qid=Q1640658|1=Kagu-tsuchi}} (Kitsuchi), the rocks that dripped from the sword solidified and were formed as the ancestor of Futsunushi. Another book is <ref name="The Age of Gods" group="Hara"/>, Kagutsuchi's blood dyed the rocks {{ill|lt=Iwasaku Nesaku|Q11287276|qid=Q11287276|1=Iwasaku and Nesaku}} (Iwazakami/Nezakami) was born, and the It is said that his son {{ill|lt=Iwatsutsuno-o|Q9010200|qid=Q9010200|lt=Iwatsutsuno-o, Iwatsutsu-no-me|1=Iwa-tsutsu-no'o}} (Iwatsutsu Otokogami and Iwatsutsu Goddess) gave birth to Futsunushi. After that, in the official history of "Nihonshoki" <ref name="Jindai shita" group="hara">"Nihonshoki" Jindai shi. </ref>, {{jalink|Takemikazuchi|Q150269 in the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=pacification of Ashihara China|1=UNKNOWN}} prior to the {{ill|lt=advent of the grandson|Q1084733|qid=Q1084733|1=Tenson kōrin}} It is said that he was dispatched to Izumo with 0}} ({{ill|lt=Kashima Shrine|Q706499|qid=Q706499|1=Kashima Jingū}} enshrined deity) and negotiated with {{ill|qid=Q276944|lt=Okuninushikami|UNKNOWN|lt=Oomi Takamikoto|1=Ōkuninushi}} to cede the country. Furthermore, Futsunushi does not appear in "{{ill|lt=Kojiki|Q813031|qid=Q813031|1=Kojiki}}".Regarding the relationship between Futsunushi and Katori, it is written in the first book of the Nihon Shoki <ref name="Jindai shita" group="Hara"/> that ``Saishūgami, this god is now in Yu Togoku Yutori no Jiya,'' and that they are worshiped as ``Katori (Katori, Katori) = Katori.'' Also, "{{ill|lt=Kogo Shui|Q531555|qid=Q531555|1=Kogo Shūi}}" (composed in {{ill|lt=Daido (Japan)|Q1373191|qid=Q1373191|lt=Daido|1=Daidō}} 2nd year ({{ill|lt=807|Q30016|qid=Q30016|1=807}}))<ref group="原">``Kogo Shui'' (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). <ref group="original"> "Kasuga Festival Norito" from "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" (completed in {{ill|lt=Extension (Japan)|UNKNOWN|lt=Extension}} 5 years ({{ill|lt=927|Q30470|qid=Q30470|1=927}})), "Kyotsu Nushikami Yunun, Ima Shimogasa Province Katori no Kami Koreya" in </ref> Kasuga Festival Article (Refer to {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref>Also, it is written as ``Katoriza Ihabishu no Mikoto''.As for the nature of the enshrined deity, Futsunushi is considered to be a god of war or war, based on the legend in the Shoki that it played an active role in pacifying the land. The word ``Hutu'' in the name is also said to be a word that expresses the sharpness of the sword, just like the name of the divine sword ``{{ill|lt=Futōmitama|Q11059754|qid=Q11059754|lt=Futunomitama|1=Futsu-no-mitama}}'' (Futōmitama/Hanirei) seen in the Kiki.{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (National History)|1983}}. The recognition of the god of war is expressed in "{{ill|lt=Ryojin Hisho|Q3010584|qid=Q3010584|1=Ryōjin Hishō}}" (late end of the {{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292|1=Heian period}}): "The god of war east of Seki, the shrine of Kashima, Katori, {{ill|lt=Suwa Taisha|Q218813|qid=Q218813|lt=Suwa|1=Suwa-taisha}}"<ref group="Hara">'Ryojin Hisho' Volume 2 Four verse divine songs. </ref> is known for the song {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. On the other hand, there is a view that due to the ancient name ``Kajitori = rudder ({{ill|lt=rudder|Q209760|qid=Q209760|1=Rudder}})'', it was worshiped as a god in charge of navigation in ancient times. In addition, there are many unknowns regarding the treatment of the different names Futsunushi and Ihahinushi (Ihahi-shu/Saishu) and the primitive rituals performed by the clans, and there are various theories including the origin of Katori-jingu Shrine (see section ``{{ill|lt=#Research|UNKNOWN|lt=Research}}'' for details).

=== Features ===
[[File:Kashima-jingu roumon.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|{{ill|lt=Kashima Shrine|Q706499|qid=Q706499|1=Kashima Jingū}} ({{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|qid=Q83273|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Kashima City|Q467471|qid=Q467471|1=Kashima, Ibaraki}})}}{{Small|{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Ichinomiya|Q1656379|qid=Q1656379|1=Ichinomiya}}. It has a deep relationship with Katori Shrine and has been called the same name since ancient times. }}]]
Katori Shrine is located in {{ill|lt=Hitachikuni|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Ichinomiya|Q1656379|qid=Q1656379|1=Ichinomiya}}'''{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kashima Shrine|1=UNKNOWN}}'''({{ill|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|Q83273|qid=Q83273|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Kashima City|Q467471|qid=Q467471|1=Kashima, Ibaraki}}, {{Coord|35|58|07.8 8|N|140|37|53.37|E|region:JP-08_type:landmark|name=Hitachikuni Ichinomiya: Kashima Shrine}}) {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Kadokawa)|1984}}<ref>``Iroha of Shrines'' (Fusosha), supervised by the Shrine Honcho, p. 76. </ref>.Both Kashima and Katori Jingu are shrines that have been deeply revered by the imperial court since ancient times. The reason for their divine power lies in the fact that both shrines were worshiped as gods of war. In ancient eastern Kanto, there were present-day {{ill|lt=Kasumigaura|Q1077984|qid=Q1077984|1=Lake Kasumigaura}} (Nishiura, {{ill|lt=Kitaura|Q11402369|qid=Q11402369|1=Kitaura}}), {{ill|lt=Inbanuma|Q5120731|qid=Q5120731|1=Inbanuma}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Teganuma|1=UNKNOWN}}, the {{ill|lt=Inland Sea|Q2578218|qid=Q2578218|1=Inland sea}} called ``{{ill|lt=Inland Sea|Q2578218|qid=Q2578218|1=Inland sea}}'' spreads out in the area that includes ``{{ill|lt=Katori Sea|Q11667182|qid=Q11667182|1=Katori Sea}}'', and both shrines are located in topographically important areas that block the entrance to it. This Katori Sea is thought to have functioned as a transportation base for the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Yamato administration|1=UNKNOWN}}'s advance into {{ill|lt=Ezo|Q932574|qid=Q932574|1=Emishi}}. </ref>, both shrines were considered to be their strongholds, and the ghosts of both shrines were enshrined in various places along the Tohoku coast as gods representing the power of the imperial court ({{ill|lt=#Katori Naesenjin|UNKNOWN|lt=described later}}).

The following examples show the importance the Imperial Court attaches to it.
* {{ill|lt=Kamigun|Q11590937|qid=Q11590937|1=Kamigun}}*: Kashima and Katori Shrines are located in {{ill|lt=Hitachikuni|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Kashima County, respectively. (Ibaraki Prefecture)|Q6374307|qid=Q6374307|lt=Kashima County|1=Kashima District, Ibaraki}} and {{ill|lt=Shimosa Province|Q1053695|qid=Q1053695|1=Shimōsa Province}}{{ill|lt=Katori County|Q780284|qid=Q780284|1=Katori District}} were designated as Kami-gun, that is, the entire county was designated as divine territory.{{Sfn|Okada|2011}} group="Original">Volume 16 of "Ryoshuikai" Selected Ordinance Doji Juden Article/Fugyo 3rd Grade and Higher Parents </ref> and {{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}<ref name="Shikibujo" group="Original"/>). There are few examples of shrines with shrines, and all of them are said to have been important locations for military and transportation {{Sfn|Okada|2011}}.
*Kashima Karatori Envoy
*: Every year, the Imperial Court sent Kashima envoys and Katori envoys, or simply Kashima Katori envoys, to both shrines {{Sfn|Okada|2011}}. Among local shrines other than Ise and Kinki, regular imperial envoys were only dispatched to {{ill|lt=Usa Jingu|Q715632|qid=Q715632|1=Usa Jingū}} (once every six years), and Kashima and Katori Jingu were extremely unusual in that they were dispatched every year.{{Sfn|Okada|2011}}.
* Name of "{{ill|lt=Jingu|Q120680118|qid=Q120680118|1=List of Jingū}}"*: "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" {{ill|lt=Engishiki Shinmyocho|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932|lt=Shinmyocho|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō}} ({{ill|lt=Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292|1=Heian period}} {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Government shrines|1=UNKNOWN}} list) There were only three shrines that were marked as "Miya Shrine": Dai Jingu ({{ill|lt=Ise Jingu|Q687168|qid=Q687168|1=Ise Grand Shrine}}{{ill|lt=Kodai Jingu|Q11581011|qid=Q11581011|lt=Naiku|1=Kōtai Jingū}}), Kashima Jingu, and Katori Jingu.{{Sfn|Okada|2011}}<ref group="Note">Before the Heian period, other examples of the use of the name ``Jingu'' include ``{{ill|lt=Ishigami Jingu|Q708859|qid=Q708859|1=Isonokami Jingū}}'' in ``Kojiki'' and ``Nihon Shoki,'' but in the ``Engishiki'' divine name book, it is written as ``Ishigami Zaburomitama Shrine'' {{Harv|Okada|2011}}. </ref>.

It is also highly revered by the {{ill|lt=Fujiwara clan|Q641628|qid=Q641628|1=Fujiwara clan}}, and {{jalink|Kasuga Taisha|Q7} in {{ill|lt=Nara|Q11444975|qid=Q11444975|1=Nara}} was founded as a shrine for the Fujiwara clan. In 14559}}, Kashima-kami was enshrined in the first hall and Katori-kami in the second hall, and they were ranked higher than {{ill|lt=Amagiya-no-Mikoto|Q2564508|qid=Q2564508|lt=Amagoyane-no-Mikoto|1=Ame-no-Koyane}} (third hall), the ancestor god of the Fujiwara clan. Even after the samurai entered the world in the Middle Ages, both shrines, which enshrine the god of war, were worshiped by the samurai. Even in modern times, faith in {{ill|lt=martial arts|Q4867842|qid=Q4867842|1=武術}} is strong, and dojos often display paired hanging scrolls with the words ``Kashima Daimyojin'' and ``Katori Daimyojin'' written on them.

=== History ===

=== Founding ===
According to the shrine's biography, it was founded in 18th year of the first Emperor Jimmu. The early period is not clear, but in ancient times it was "{{ill|lt=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki|Q11481687|qid=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}" (written in the early 8th century). </ref> already mentions a branch shrine as ``Katori Mikonosha'', and it is certain that it was enshrined before that <ref name="Katori Heritage"/>.

Also, in ancient times, Katori Shrine is said to have functioned as a base for the control of eastern Japan by the Yamato Imperial Court, along with {{ill|lt=Kashima Shrine|Q706499|qid=Q706499|1=Kashima Jingū}}, so there is a theory that it was founded when the Imperial Court enshrined both shrines as a base. On the other hand, there is also a theory that the original ritual existed before that time (see section ``{{ill|lt=#Research|UNKNOWN|lt=Research}}'').

=== Shinto priest ===

==== Job system ====
Regarding the official structure of the shrine, "{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" was established in {{ill|lt=Extension (Japan)|UNKNOWN|lt=Extension}} 5 years ({{ill|lt=927|Q30470|qid=Q30470|1=927}}) <ref group="Hara">``Engishiki'' Volume 15, Kashima Katori-jo (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref><ref group="Hara">"Engishiki" Volume 3 Extraordinary Festival Katori Musician Costume Article (Refer to {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref><ref group="Hara">"Engishiki" Volume 3 Extraordinary Festival Jinguji Kirokujo (Refer to {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). </ref> records one chief priest, one Negi, two monoki, as well as six musicians and eight maiko, and says that the chief priest is in the same rank as {{ill|lt=Jūhachii|Q11488720|qid=Q11488720|1=Junior Eighth Rank}}. {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}

The priests that can be seen from the end of the Heian period to the Middle Ages are Ōnegi, Ōgūji, vice-gishi, monoshin-gi, gyosho-negi, national ceremonials, gonnegi, tadokoro, ansu, bunshiji, daishu, and kenpei. There are more than 100 names, including Kaishu, Miyasuke, Rokujidai, Sokengyo, Gonnosuke, Seikenbikaishu, and Takakuramedai.{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}.

Prior to the Meiji period, the central priests of shrine rituals were the Ryōshagami (Grand Priest, Onegi), the Six Officials (Miyanosuke, Gonegi, Monshingi, National Events, Grand Festival, Vice Festival), as well as Sokengyo and Gonnosuke.・He was the ruler of Gyoki Negi, Rokujidai, Tadokoro, Ansu, Takakuramedai, Seikenbibishi, Gonkenbibishi, Bunishi, etc.{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}.

==== Ritual Clan ====
The clan that performed rituals at the shrine is said to have been the ``Katori clan'' (Katori clan) in ancient times {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Kadokawa)|1984}}. "Katori Daiguji Genealogy" <ref> Included in the 7th volume of "Zokugun Doshoju". According to </ref>, its founder was Naemasu no Mikoto, Amanaeka-no-Mikoto, the son of Futsunushi (Ketsunushi), and lived for {{ill|lt=Emperor Bidatsu|Q316637|qid=Q316637|1=Emperor Bidatsu}} ({{ill|lt=572 years|Q49189|qid=Q49189|1=572}}? - {{ill|lt=Emperor Bunmu|Q357246|qid=Q357246|1=Emperor Monmu}} ({{ill|lt=697|Q23489|qid=Q23489|1=697}} - It is said that he began enshrining Katori Shrine in {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Kadokawa)|1984}}.

In this way, the Katori clan was a family that claimed to be the descendants of Futsunushi, {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=47}}, and later, according to the same genealogy, '''{{ill|lt=Onakatomi clan|Q11431853|qid=Q11431853|1=Ōnakatomi clan}}''' was descended from Onakatomi Kiyonobu. It is said that he was adopted by Ren Gohyakushima and became Katori Daiguji, and Kiyonobu's son Akio took charge of Katori Ominegi ({{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Kadokawa)|1984}} (however, the reliability of the names and dates is low {{Sfn|Matsuo|2014|pp=260-265}}). From then on, until the end of the Heian period, the Onakatomi clan had a monopoly on both the chief priest and Ominegi {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Kadokawa)|1984}}. However, since Katori-jingu Shrine was the guardian deity of the Fujiwara clan, the Fujiwara clan in the center was in charge of its replacement {{Sfn|Katori-jingu Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. {{clear}}In the first year of {{ill|lt=Koharu|Q1194459|qid=Q1194459|1=Kōji (Heian period)}} ({{ill|lt=1142|Q19614|qid=Q19614|1=1142}}), the Nakatomi clan of Kashima Shrine's chief priest passed away to Katori Shrine. After he was appointed as Daiguji, there was a conflict between the Katori Onakatomi clan and the Kashima Nakatomi clan over Katori's position as Daiguji {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. The two clans fought against each other by lobbying the Kamakura shogunate and the Sekkan family, and in the end, the Onakatomi clan won around the {{ill|lt=Hiroki|Q1194200|qid=Q1194200|1=Kangi}} years ({{ill|lt=1229|Q5411|qid=Q5411|1=1229}} - {{ill|lt=1232|Q5418|qid=Q5418|1=1232}}) {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}.

Around this time, the influence of the Fujiwara clan began to fade, and conflicts developed within the Onakatomi clan over the chief priest, Oune no Yoshiki, and the territory of the shrine. This conflict came to an end around {{ill|lt=Oan|Q1146245|qid=Q1146245|1=Ōan}} 7 ({{ill|lt=1374|Q6269|qid=Q6269|1=1374}}), and the end of the Kamakura and Muromachi periods were stabilized with the One no Yoshiie taking the initiative {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. After that, in the early modern period, it came under the control of the Edo shogunate, but it is said that there were repeated conflicts {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}.

=== Company territory ===
"{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}" <ref name="Shikibu-jo" group="Hara">"Engishiki" Volume 18 Shikibu-jo Gunji-jo (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). According to </ref>, {{ill|lt=Shimosa Province|Q1053695|qid=Q1053695|1=Shimōsa Province}}{{ill|lt=Katori District|Q780284|qid=Q780284|1=Katori District}}, where the Jingu is located, was {{ill|lt=Kamigun|Q11590937|qid=Q11590937|1=Kamigun}}, that is, the entire district was designated as the divine territory of the Jingu. "{{ill|lt=Hitachikuni Fudoki|Q11481687|qid=Q11481687|1=Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki}}" <ref group="Hara">"Hitachikuni Fudoki" Kashima-gunjo. </ref> is located in {{ill|lt=Hitachikuni|Q1055353|qid=Q1055353|1=Hitachi Province}}{{ill|lt=Kashima County, where Kashima Shrine is located. (Ibaraki Prefecture)|Q6374307|qid=Q6374307|lt=Kashima County|1=Kashima District, Ibaraki}} (Koshima District) was a god in {{ill|lt=Taika|Q1077930|qid=Q1077930|1=Taika (era)}}5 ({{ill|lt=649|Q31117|qid=Q31117|1=649}}) It is said that Katori County was established as a county, and it is assumed that Katori County was established in the same way.

{{ill|lt=Daido (Japan)|Q1373191|qid=Q1373191|lt=Daido|1=Daidō}} 1st year ({{ill|lt=806|Q30021|qid=Q30021|1=806}}) <ref group="Hara"> Shinsho Kaku Chofusho 10 Shinto rituals and feudal families Daido 1st year (806) (see {{Harvnb|Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection}}). According to </ref>, there were 70 gates in the shrine {{Sfn|Sharyo (National History)|1983}}. In the 11th century, there are also articles about fief donations from the Fujiwara clan {{Sfn|Sharyo (National History)|1983}}.In the {{ill|lt=Middle Ages|Q12554|qid=Q12554|1=Middle Ages}}, there were conflicts between priests and invasions of divine territory by the samurai families represented by the {{ill|lt=Chiba clan|Q2975237|qid=Q2975237|1=Chiba clan}}, and lawsuits were frequently held {{Sfn|Sharyo (National History)|1983}}. Also, as a special income that began in the Middle Ages, there was an offering from ``Kaifu'', that is, fishermen in the Katori Sea.

After the fall of the Chiba clan, under {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|qid=Q171977|1=Tokugawa Ieyasu}} who entered the Kanto region in {{ill|lt=Tensho|Q1145058|qid=Q1145058|1=Tenshō (Momoyama period)}} ({{ {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. As a result, the shrine territory was significantly reduced, and in the same year, 1,000 koku was given as {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=shuinji|1=UNKNOWN}} {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. According to historical sources from the Genroku period, the area was worth 900 koku of Jingu territory, 100 koku of Oto Shrine territory, and 20 koku of Jingu Temple territory {{Sfn|Sharyo (National History)|1983}}.

In addition, {{ill|lt=Masakazu|Q1324807|qid=Q1324807|1=Shōwa (1312–1317)}}5 ({{ill|lt=1316|Q5744|qid=Q5744|1=1316}}), Oei 31st ({{ill|lt=1424|Q6276|qid=Q6276|1=1424}}), {{ill|lt=Civilization (Japan)|Q1193544|qid=Q1193544|lt=Bunmei|1=Bunmei}} There are also historical sources that say it was built in 15 years ({{ill|lt=1483|Q6637|qid=Q6637|1=1483}}) and 1st year of {{ill|lt=Meio|Q1193841|qid=Q1193841|1=Meiō}} ({{ill|lt=1492|Q6679|qid=Q6679|1=1492}}.{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Kadokawa)|1984}}. In this way, during the Kamakura period, the temple was rebuilt approximately once every 20 years, but it becomes difficult to do so after the Nanbokucho period, and not many historical materials remain from that period.{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Kadokawa)|1984}}During the Edo period, the shogunate constructed a large-scale construction of Katori Shrine (Kadokawa) in 12 years ({{ill|lt=1607|Q6756|qid=Q6756|1=1607}}). It was rebuilt in {{ill|lt=Genroku|Q1325001|qid=Q1325001|1=Genroku}}13 ({{ill|lt=1700|Q6813|qid=Q6813|1=1700}}), and the main shrine buildings including the main hall from this time remain to this day.{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Kadokawa)|1984}}.

The current form of the main shrine is ``Asame-dono'' (ref name="Asame" group="note"). <ref name="Fusa"/>{{Sfn|Miura|1986}} is said to convey the format of ``</ref>''. Asame-den is a shrine that once existed at the shrine, and is usually used as {{ill|lt=Iwasaku Nesaku|Q11287276|qid=Q11287276|lt=Iwasaku-kami/Ne-saku-kami|1=Iwasaku and Nesaku}} (the grandparent god of Tsunetsu no Kami). ), and was used as a temporary shrine (karido: a shrine building where a divine object is temporarily enshrined) during the Shikinen Sengu of the main shrine (main shrine).{{Sfn|Miura|1986}} During that time, a temporary Asame-den was also built to enshrine the gods Iwasaki and Nesaki.{{Sfn|Miura|1986}}. It is thought that the last main shrine was built in 1330 during the Kamakura period, and that subsequent main shrines inherited the form of Asameden.{{Sfn|Miura|1986}}As mentioned above, Asame-den played an important role at Katori Shrine, but its existence was only confirmed until the Middle Ages, and it has been pointed out that it is likely to have been abolished in the early modern period {{Sfn|Yamaguchi|2013}}. The format of the Asame-den was an abbreviated version of the main shrine, and its formality declined as a result of its omission. However, at Katori Shrine, after the 2nd year of Gentoku, the situation continued for a long period in which it was difficult to construct the main shrine, and during that time, Asame-den It is presumed that the Me-den had to be used as a substitute for the Sei-den, and it is also pointed out that the form of the Sei-den was partially introduced into Asame-den with no hope of restoration of the Sei-den.{{Sfn|Yamaguchi|2013}} In other words, changes in the format of Asame-den have been confirmed to raise the formality of the shrine, and these trends appear to have influenced the current format of the main shrine {{Sfn|Yamaguchi|2013}}.

Regarding the main temple of the Kamakura period, it is estimated from ancient documents that it was ``a building with a flat gabled structure with five-ken columns and two beams, and an eave on the back side,'' and based on the existence of Shiki-nen remodeling, it is assumed that this style dates back to the early Heian period {{Sfn|Miura|1986}}.

=== Precincts ===
The hill on which the shrine is located is called ``Kamegaseyama'' because of its low center and high surroundings {{Sfn|Katori Koji|1995|p=50}}

The shrine precincts are considered a sacred area and have untouched nature, so there are many giant cedar trees, as well as large Japanese fir, fir, and black pine trees. Many plants grow not only in the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=tall tree layer|1=UNKNOWN}} but also in the sub-tall tree layer, shrub layer, and forest floor, and it is one of the prefecture's oldest old cedar forests and has been designated as a natural monument by Chiba Prefecture.

=== Shrine building ===
[[File:Katori-jingu honden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Main shrine (National Important Cultural Property)}}{{Small|From the northeast. Facing the back left is the worship hall. }}]]
[[File:Katori-jingu romon.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Romon (National Important Cultural Property)}}]]
[[File:Katori-jingu kyuhaiden.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Prayer Hall (Former Worship Hall)<br />(Chiba Prefecture Designated Cultural Property)}}]]
The current main shrine building was built in {{ill|lt=Genroku|Q1325001|qid=Q1325001|1=Genroku}}13 of the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963|1=Edo period}} ({{ill|lt=1700|Q6813|qid=Q6813|1=1700}}) by order of {{ill|lt=Tokugawa Tsunayoshi|Q313745|qid=Q313745|1=Tokugawa Tsunayoshi}}, the fifth shogun of the Edo shogunate. At this time, the main shrine, worship hall, and tower gate were constructed, but the worship hall was renovated during major renovations from 1936 to 1940, and is currently used as a prayer hall. During this major renovation in the Showa period, a shrine hall and a shrine were also constructed. The main shrine buildings, both before and after the major renovation, are '''{{ill|lt=Gongen-zukuri|Q3155268|qid=Q3155268|1=Ishi-no-ma-zukuri}}''', which consists of a main hall, a hall of worship, and a hall of worship. Of the above, the main shrine and tower gate are designated as important cultural properties of the country, the former worship hall (prayer hall) is designated as a cultural property designated by Chiba Prefecture, and the current worship hall is registered as a registered tangible cultural property of the country.The main shrine was built in 1700. Sangensha {{ill|lt=Ryuzo|Q210684|qid=Q210684|1=Nagare-zukuri}}, {{ill|lt=cypress bark roof|Q90373477|qid=Q90373477|1=cypress bark roof}}, facing south. It is one of the largest shrines of this type<ref name="Fusa"/>. The front eaves are brought into the room, and there is also a short eave at the back <ref name="Fusa"/>. When it was designated as an important cultural property, it was written as ``nagaru-zukuri'', but because it has an eave on the back, it is considered to be a type of ryo-ryu-zukuri {{Sfn|Miura|1986}}. The walls and pillars are painted black lacquer, giving it a distinctive black-based appearance. The roof is currently made of cypress bark, but it is said that it was once made of persimmon bark. </ref>. The style is representative of the early modern period {{ill|lt=Early modern|Q5308718|qid=Q5308718|1=Early modern period}}, and while the Momoyama style can be seen in many parts, the Keicho period techniques are also incorporated.<ref name="Fusa"/> During the major renovations in the Showa era, the main shrine was also extensively repaired {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. Regarding this main shrine, there is the Asame-dono, which once existed in the shrine. In addition to being thought to inherit the shrine called "group="note"/>" (see section "{{ill|lt=#Shrine construction|UNKNOWN|lt=Shrine construction}}"), in the normal Ryoryu-zukuri style, the shrine inside the main shrine is the main shrine (large beam). It has been pointed out that it is an unusual form in that it is located in the back eave (the part that attaches to the periphery of the building), whereas it is located in the main part of the architectural structure (the main part of the building where the building is built) {{Sfn|Miura|1986}} (see the figure below).The ``Worship Hall'', ``Hideden'', and ``Shinsensho'' were built during major renovations during the Showa period. It is a one-story wooden building with a cypress bark roof. </ref>. It is connected from the front of the main hall to the Heiden and Worship Hall, and has a Gongen-zukuri style <ref name="Fusa"/>. In addition, there is a houndstooth gable in front of the shrine. Until then, the worship hall (old worship hall) had been painted red, but in this construction, the shaft was painted with black lacquer, and the kumimono and toma mata were painted in rich colors, giving it a new appearance that was in proportion to the main shrine.``Romon'' was built in 1700. It is a three-room, one-family building with a gabled structure. The roof is currently roofed with copper sheets, but originally it was {{ill|lt=shingle roofing|UNKNOWN|lt=chestnut roofing}} (Tochibuki) <ref name="Treasure">[http://www.katori-jingu.or.jp/houmotu.htm Treasures and Cultural Properties] (official website). </ref>. The style is pure Japanese, and the walls and pillars are tan lacquered. The statues inside the tower gate are commonly referred to as ``Minister of the Left and Minister of the Right,'' but it is said that the one on the right is {{ill|lt=Takeuchi Sukune|Q1073668|qid=Q1073668|1=Takenouchi no Sukune}} and the one on the left is {{ill|lt=Fujiwara Kamatari|Q433995|qid=Q433995|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}}<ref name="Treasure"/>. Also, the plaque on the tower is the brush of {{ill|lt=Heihachiro Togo|Q296785|qid=Q296785|1=Tōgō Heihachirō}}<ref name="Treasure"/>. This tower gate is positioned as a symbolic building of the shrine <ref name="treasure"/>.

'''Prayer Hall'' ('''Old Worship Hall'') was built in 1700. It was built and used as a worship hall, but was moved to the southeast during major renovations in the Showa era, and then moved approximately 1.5 meters further west in 1984 ({{ill|lt=1984|Q2432|qid=Q2432|1=1984}}). It is a gambrel-style house with a width of 5 ken and a depth of 3 ken. The roof is currently made of copper sheets, but it was originally made of tochibuki, which was changed in 1965. The walls and pillars are tan lacquered. It is relatively large-scale for a worship hall, and the style at the time of its construction is shown in the carvings and other details.In addition to the above, the shrine was built in Meiji 42 ({{ill|lt=1909|Q2057|qid=Q2057|1=1909}}), and is a wooden {{ill|lt=school warehouse|Q2875112|qid=Q2875112|1=Azekura-zukuri}} (a cultural property designated by Katori City) {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=56}}. Jintokukan was built in 1961 ({{ill|lt=1961|Q3696|qid=Q3696|1=1961}}) and stands on the site of the former Daiguji's residence{{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=56}}. The gate (Imperial Envoy Gate) was a repurposed front gate of the former Daiguji's residence, and was built in the first year of {{ill|lt=Tenmei|Q1194121|qid=Q1194121|1=Tenmei}} ({{ill|lt=1781|Q7719|qid=Q7719|1=1781}}), {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=55}}, three-length girder, two-length beam, single-story, gabled structure. The roof is thatched and has a fence on both sides (Chiba Prefecture-designated cultural property) |publisher=Chiba Prefectural Office |date=2022-02-10 |accessdate=2022-02-12}}</ref>. In addition, Kaunkaku, which stands in the northeast, was built in 1896 ({{ill|lt=1896|Q7846|qid=Q7846|1=1896}}) and is a registered tangible cultural property of the country.

=== Keystone ===
[[File:Katori-jingu kanameishi.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|{{ill|lt=Keystone|Q11630053|qid=Q11630053|1=Kaname-ishi}} Shrine}}]]
[[File:Kaname-ishi-stone,katori-jingu,katori-city.japan.JPG|thumb|150px|right|{{Center|Shape of the keystone}}]]
'''{{ill|lt=Keystone|Q11630053|qid=Q11630053|1=Kaname-ishi}}''' (Kanameishi) is a spiritual stone located in the west of the temple grounds. The shape is convex.

It was once thought that earthquakes were caused by {{ill|lt=large catfish|Q257275|qid=Q257275|1=Namazu}} (catfish) that lived underground. The keystone is still passed down today as a guardian deity that protects the large catfish from earthquakes. The Kashima/Katori keystone is said to be a stake that holds the head and tail of a giant catfish, and although it looks small, it is said that the part underground is so large that it can never be removed. When {{ill|lt=Teikyo|Q1146221|qid=Q1146221|1=Jōkyō}} visited the shrine in the first year of the year ({{ill|lt=1684|Q7654|qid=Q7654|1=1684}}), {{ill|lt=Mitsukuni|Tokugawa|qid=Tokugawa|ltq=Q1194944}} had him dig around the key stone, but he was unable to reach the root.{{Sfn|Katori Koji|1995|p=63}}. Additionally, there is a concave keystone at {{ill|lt=Kashima Jingu|Q706499|qid=Q706499|1=Kashima Jingū}}, and a similar story is told.

=== Others ===
[[File:Katori-jingu sannotorii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Three Torii}}]]
[[File:Training ship Katori's anchor.jpg|thumb|Training ship Katori's anchor]]
* Sacred Tree - The large cedar tree that stands in front of the worship hall is said to be 1,000 years old {{Sfn|Katori Koji|1995|p=52}}.
* Scout Cedar (Monomi no Sugi) - A cedar that {{ill|lt=Minamoto no Yoriyoshi|Q3082851|qid=Q3082851|1=Minamoto no Yoriyoshi}} had his scouts climb.
* Sanbonsugi - A cedar tree that is said to have been split into three parts due to Minamoto no Yoriyoshi's prayer (one tree is dead) {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=52}}. It is said that Minamoto no Yoriyoshi prayed to this cedar for ``the peace of the world, the prosperity of the head of the shrine, and the longevity of his descendants.''
* Kibosugi - Standing to the left of the tower gate. When Tokugawa Mitsukuni visited the shrine in 1684, it was named because it was the mother of the many cedar trees that stood within the precincts (currently withered) {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=50}}.
* Komonzakura - A cherry tree said to have been hand-planted by Tokugawa Mitsukuni when he visited the shrine in 1684 (currently the {{ill|lt=蘖|Q960522|qid=Q960522|lt=Hikobee|1=Basal shoot}} has grown) {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=51}}.
* Emperor Taisho's hand-planted pine tree - A hand-planted pine tree {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=51}} when {{ill|lt=Emperor Taisho|Q157052|qid=Q157052|1=Emperor Taishō}} visited the shrine on May 21, 1911|Q2076}} during the {{ill|lt=Crown Prince|Q207293|qid=Q207293|1=Crown prince}} era.* Hitachinomiya Teuematsu - A hand-planted pine tree that was planted by {{ill|lt=Prince Hitachinomiya Masahito|Q725680|qid=Q725680|1=Masahito, Prince Hitachi}} when he visited the shrine on April 7, 1966 ({{ill|lt=1966|Q2649|qid=Q2649|1=1966}}).
* {{ill|lt=Maritime Self-Defense Force|Q731647|qid=Q731647|1=Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force}}{{ill|lt=Training ship|Q11608028|qid=Q11608028|1=military training ship}}{{ill|lt=Katori (training ship)|Q11263982|qid=Q11263982|lt=Katori|1=JDS Katori}}'s anchor
* Kamiike
* Sakurababa - You can see Mt. Tsukuba, Mt. Kashima, Katorigaura, Itako Islands, etc.
*Deer Garden - In 2015, sacred deer were transferred to [https://katorideer.webnode.jp/ Katori Deer Protection Society] and are kept on the grounds.
*
* Amagozuka - Near Okumiya. This is said to be the site of a platform used to pray for rain during the drought of the 4th year of Tenpyo ({{ill|lt=732|Q23569|qid=Q23569|1=732}}).{{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=62}}

=== Approach ===
There are two approaches to the shrine, each with a torii gate.

Omotesando is the approach to the shrine that continues from the former center of Sawara City, and corresponds to the current {{ill|lt=Chiba Prefectural Route 55 Sawara Yamada Line|Q11406638|qid=Q11406638|lt=Prefectural Route 55|1=Chiba Prefectural Road Route 55}}. Ichino Torii stands near the intersection with {{ill|lt=Chiba Prefectural Route 56 Sawara Tsubakikai Line|Q11406639|qid=Q11406639|lt=Prefectural Route 56|1=Chiba Prefectural Road Route 56}} ({{Coord|35|53|15.71|N|140|30|41.09|E|region:JP-12_type:landmark|name=Ichino Torii}}). The distance from the first torii gate to the second torii gate is approximately 1.6km along the road.Another approach begins in Tsumiya, Katori City. The starting point of this approach is the Tone Riverbank, and there is a Hamatorii gate facing the river ({{Coord|35|54|05.82|N|140|31|34.12|E|region:JP-12_type:landmark|name=Tsumiya Hamatorii}}). It is said that the name torii derives from the fact that the enshrined deity came ashore from here, and the road from this torii was once Omotesando {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=57}}. "{{ill|lt=Koyuki|Q11459316|qid=Q11459316|1=Shōyūki}}" {{ill|lt=Koyuki|Koyuki|qid=Koyuki|ltq=Q11459316}} Article of 3rd year of security (era name)|Q1150852|Security}} ({{ill|lt=1023|Q19263|qid=Q19263|1=1023}}) According to </ref>, the Kashima envoy ({{ill|lt=Hohei|Q11445508|qid=Q11445508|lt=Hohei envoy|1=Hōhei}} from the imperial court) left Kashima Jingu Shrine and went to Katori Shrine, and it is said that it was a regular practice for him to cross the sea to Katori Shrine for offerings.{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. Even today, during the Shikinen Shinko Festival, a barge carrying a mikoshi departs from here {{Sfn|Katori Koji|1995|p=57}}. Also, near the torii gate, there is a night light (a cultural property designated by Katori City) that is a remnant of the prosperity of shipping in the past. </ref>, {{ill|lt=Akiko Yosano|Q464104|qid=Q464104|1=Yosano Akiko}}There is a poem monument. It is approximately 2.5km along the road to the second torii gate. Along the way, the outer shrines of the precincts, such as Shinojin Shrine, Tsunio Shrine, and Okinomiya Shrine, are enshrined.Also, at the end of the approach to the shrine, the approach now continues from the second torii gate to the tower gate, but in ancient times, Omotesando was the road that curved at right angles in front of the tower gate and continued to Okugu-mae in the west. Katori Shrine, Ichinomiya Shrine in Shimousa Province] (Katori City website ``Katori Heritage''). </ref>.

=== Setsusha ===
There are a total of 30 Setsusha shrines, 9 Setsusha shrines (3 shrines within the precincts, 6 shrines outside the precincts) and 21 Setsusha shrines (7 shrines within the precincts, 14 shrines outside the precincts).<ref>The Setsusha shrines are based on the Shinshu Katori Jingu Short History, pp. 35-40. </ref>.

=== Sessha ===
{{List of coordinates|Section=Setsusha}}
Sessha was officially established by a notification from {{ill|lt=Ministry of the Interior (Japan)|Q1142265|qid=Q1142265|lt=Ministry of the Interior|1=Home Ministry}} on March 21, 1877 ({{ill|lt=1877|Q7773|qid=Q7773|1=1877}}).

[[File:Kashimashingu-sha (Katori-jingu)-2.jpg|thumb|170px|right|{{Center|Kashimashingusha}}]]

: "Kashimashingusha". Precinct Setsusha ({{Coord|35|53|11.71|N|140|31|44.49|E|region:JP-12_type:landmark|name=Precinct Setsusha: Kashima Shingu Shrine}}) is located at the rear right of the main shrine. Takematsuchijin is the enshrined deity of {{ill|lt=Kashima Shrine|Q706499|qid=Q706499|1=Kashima Jingū}}.

:* Enshrined deity: unknown
:* Annual festival: {{ill|lt=December 7th|Q2299|qid=Q2299|1=December 7}}: "Soba Takajinja". Formerly {{ill|lt=Gosha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316|1=Gō-sha}} in Kyotogaisetsusha. It is a deeply related shrine that has been called the "First Sesshuya" since ancient times, and like the main shrine, it is said to have been founded in the 18th year of Emperor Jimmu. Sodaka Shrine] (Katori City website “Katori Heritage”). </ref>. The enshrined deity has been considered a mystery since ancient times, and it is still unclear even today {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=35}}. There is a legend in our company that, at the command of Katori no kami, Sodaka no kami stole horses from Mutsu no kami and became a horse herder, and the relationship with the Ezo conquest and the role of Katori Jingu have been pointed out. </ref>. The main shrine was built in the early Edo period and is designated as a prefectural cultural property, and the Hidenade Festival is designated as an intangible folk cultural property by Katori City.

; Okumiya
:* Enshrinement location: Katori, Katori City ({{Coord|35|53|03.51|N|140|31|35.37|E|region:JP-12_type:landmark|name=Kyotogaisha: Okumiya}})

The shrine building uses old materials from the {{ill|lt=Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168|qid=Q687168|1=Ise Grand Shrine}}{{ill|lt=sengu|Q2271023|qid=Q2271023|1=Sengū}} in 1973 ({{ill|lt=1973|Q2477|qid=Q2477|1=1973}}) {{Sfn|Katori Koji|1995|p=37}}.

; Matami Shrine
:* Enshrinement location: Katori, Katori City ({{Coord|35|53|10.80|N|140|31|20.83|E|region:JP-12_type:landmark|name=Outside shrine: Matami Shrine}})
:* Deities enshrined: {{ill|lt=Amanae no Mikoto|Q1704940|qid=Q1704940|1=Ame no Naemasu no Mikoto}} (Ame no Naemasu no Mikoto), Takenui no Mikoto (Takenui no Mikoto), {{ill|lt=Amenoshimo no Mikoto|Q91088537|qid=Q91088537|lt=Ame no Oshikumo no Mikoto|1=Ame-no-Oshikumone}} (Ame no Oshikumo no Mikoto)
:* Annual festival: {{ill|lt=February 20th|Q2344|qid=Q2344|1=February 20}}
: "Mata mijinja". Kyoto Gaisetsusha. The enshrined deity, Amanaekamei, is the son of the Tsunetsu no kami and is said to be the ancestral deity of the Katori clan. For this reason, it is also called "Wakamiko Shrine" {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=5}}. Bunumai-no-Mikoto is the son of Kashima no Mikoto, and Tenshigumo-no-Mikoto is the son of Amagoyane-no-Mikoto. The stone chamber of the tumulus remains exposed on the right side of the main shrine, and has been designated as a historic site by Katori City as the ``Matami tumulus.''

; Shinobu Shrine
:* Enshrinement location: Tsunomiya, Katori City ({{Coord|35|53|54.33|N|140|31|36.81|E|region:JP-12_type:landmark|name=Gaijo-setsusha: Shinojin Shrine}}):* Enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Izanagi|Q813858|qid=Q813858|lt=Izanagi Mikoto|1=Izanagi}} (Izanagi Mikoto)
: "Oshiojinja". Also known as "East Palace" {{Sfn|Katori Koji|1995|p=36}}. A shrine outside the precincts that is located to the east of Tsutsuo Shrine. In ancient times, it is said that summer exorcisms were performed here {{Sfn|Katori Koji|1995|p=36}}. It is said that until the 17th year of the Meiji era ({{ill|lt=1884|Q7819|qid=Q7819|1=1884}}), a festival was held in which the identity of horses captured in Mutsu was confessed as a ``white confession festival,'' and similar to the legend at Sodaka Shrine, a connection with the pursuit of Ezo was suggested <ref name="illustration"/>.

:* Enshrined deity: {{ill|lt=Ame no Tajikarao|Q849412|qid=Q849412|lt=Tentate Riki Otokami|1=Ame-no-Tajikarao}} (Ame no Tajikara Onokami)
:* Annual festival: {{ill|lt=April 7th|Q2505|qid=Q2505|1=April 7}}: "Odojinja". Formerly {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=kensha|1=Ken-sha|qid=Q90139226}}. {{ill|lt=Emperor Keiko|Q329723|qid=Q329723|1=Emperor Keikō}} It is said that it was founded in 40 years. </ref>. The three Raryūo-membres, Nosori-membres, and three Japanese-style mirrors have been designated as tangible cultural properties by Chiba Prefecture.

; Returneda Shrine
:* Enshrinement location: Katori City Kaeda ({{Coord|35|51|45.46|N|140|30|59.96|E|region:JP-12|name=Kaeda Shrine}})
:* Deities enshrined: {{ill|lt=Kagutsuchi|Q1640658|qid=Q1640658|lt=Kagutsuchi no kami|1=Kagu-tsuchi}} (Kagutsuchi no kami), {{ill|lt=Hannyasu|Q9285919|qid=Q9285919|lt=Haniyasu Hime no kami|1=Haniyasu-hiko and Haniyasu-hime}} (Haniyasuhime no kami): "Kayada Jinja". Formerly {{ill|lt=Murasha|Q134917284|qid=Q134917284|1=Son-sha}}. Like the main shrine, it is said to have been founded in the 18th year of Emperor Jimmu, and is also mentioned in the ``Chiba Prefecture Place Names'' (Heibonsha) section on Kaeda Shrine. </ref>, the name ``Kaeda Akuoji Shrine'' can be seen in ancient documents from the Kamakura period. </ref>. Inside the shrine grounds, there are stone shrines dedicated to Shokoku Ichinomiya <ref name="Kaeda"/>. The main shrine was built in the Edo period and is designated as a tangible cultural property by Chiba Prefecture.

=== Festival ===

=== Shikinen Festival ===
[[File:Jinko Festival,Tsunomiya,Katori Jingu Shrine,Katori-city,Japan.JPG|thumb|200px|right|{{Center|Shikinen Shinko Festival (2014)}}]]
As the grand festival of Shikinen, ``Shikinenjin Kosai'' is held once every 12 years in the year of the horse. The Shinko Festival in front of the precincts is held on April 15th every year, but the Shikinen Taisai Festival is held on a large scale on both April 15th and 16th. In ancient times, it was also called the ``War God Festival'' or ``Gunjin Festival'' {{Sfn|Katori War God Festival (National History)|1983}}.

This festival is said to be a model of the pacification of the eastern provinces by the chief deity Tsunetsu.{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. It was originally called the ``Shikinen Sengu Grand Festival'' and was held to coincide with the Shikinen construction that takes place once every 20 years. However, like the Shikinen construction, it declined around the time of the {{ill|lt=Onin War|Q385676|qid=Q385676|1=Ōnin War}}, and it last disappeared in {{ill|lt=Eiroku|Q1143341|qid=Q1143341|1=Eiroku}}11 ({{ill|lt=1568|Q6648|qid=Q6648|1=1568}}) until the Meiji period {{Sfn|Katori Gunjin Festival (National History)|1983}}. Afterwards, it was revived in the 8th year of Meiji ({{ill|lt=1875|Q7764|qid=Q7764|1=1875}}) and was held every year, but from 1882 ({{ill|lt=1882|Q7812|qid=Q7812|1=1882}}) onwards, it was decided that it would be held every year of the horse, and it continues to this day {{Sfn|Katori Gunjin Festival (National History)|1983}}.

The flow of the festival is as follows {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=26}}.* 15th: A parade of shrines centered around mikoshi departs from Jingu and arrives at Tsunomiya. The mikoshi was transferred to a barge on the banks of the Tone River, and a festival was held on the boat. Next was the welcome festival at Kashima Shrine. After going up the Tone River and landing at the Sawara Estuary, we stayed overnight at {{ill|lt=Otabisho|Q11489117|qid=Q11489117|1=Otabisho}}.
* 16th: The Shinko train toured the city and returned to the shrine by land.

[[File:Rice-transplanting Festival in Katori-jingu 1,katori-city,japan.jpg|thumb|180px|right|{{Center|[[Katori Shrine Rice-transplanting Festival|Rice-transplanting Festival]]}}]]
; {{ill|lt=Katori Shrine Rice Planting Festival|Q11667185|qid=Q11667185|lt=Orice Planting Festival|1=Otaue Festival at Katori Jingū}}
: "Otauesai". Held on the first Saturday and Sunday in April. The plowing ceremony is held on the first day, and the rice planting ceremony is held on the second day, both of which are major festivals. A festival to pray for a rich harvest by planting rice in the shrine's Saida area. According to historical sources, it was already seen in {{ill|lt=Meitoku|Q1145032|qid=Q1145032|1=Meitoku}} 2nd year ({{ill|lt=1391|Q6378|qid=Q6378|1=1391}}), {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=29}}, and the festival is counted as one of Japan's three major rice planting festivals.<ref group="Note">``Japan's Three Great Rice Planting Festivals'' are held at Katori Shrine, {{ill|lt=Izanomiya|Q10885171|qid=Q10885171|1=Izawa-no-miya}} ({{ill|lt=Mie Prefecture|Q128196|qid=Q128196|1=Mie Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Shima City|Q338009|qid=Q338009|1=Shima, Mie}}, {{ill|lt=Isobe Shrine) Kanda|Q11588063|qid=Q11588063|1=Isobe-no-Omita}}), {{ill|lt=Sumiyoshi Taisha|Q705949|qid=Q705949|1=Sumiyoshi-taisha}} ({{ill|lt=Osaka Prefecture|Q122723|qid=Q122723|1=Osaka Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Osaka City|Q35765|qid=Q35765|1=Osaka}}, {{ill|lt=Sumiyoshi's rice planting|Q11381803|qid=Q11381803|1=Sumiyoshi-no-Otaue Festival}}). </ref><ref name="Spring"/>. For more information, see "{{ill|lt=Katori Shrine Rice Planting Festival|Q11667185|qid=Q11667185|1=Otaue Festival at Katori Jingū}}".

;Regular festival/Shinko festival: Held on April 14th and 15th. Both are big festivals. The annual festival is the most important festival at the shrine. Since the shrine is one of the {{ill|lt=Imperial shrines|Q175288|qid=Q175288|1=Chokusaisha}}, it is visited by imperial envoys once every six years (years of the Rat and Year of the Horse){{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=25}}. The Shinko Festival is held the day after the regular festival, where a procession of Shinko wearing Heian period-style costumes marches forward, and the Gotairi Festival is held in the parking lot. </ref>.

; great feast
: "Daikyosai". It will be held on November 30th. Middle festival. This festival is said to be based on the fact that Takemikazuchi, the chief deity of Tsunetsu, cared for the gods when he subdued the land.{{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=33}} It is held after sunset, and many rare offerings are offered to the shrine <ref>[http://www.katori-jingu.or.jp/siki_winter.htm autumn] (official website) </ref>.

; Dango festival
: "Dunkisai". It will be held on December 7th. Middle festival. Also known as the ``Yaishi Yato Dango Festival,'' this is a festival of thanksgiving for a bountiful harvest in which dango made from new grains are offered. More than 80 round dango are offered to the shrine. Because there is no offering of divine sake, it is said to be a festival to honor Hime, the deity who entertained the gods at the grand festival. </ref>. After the festival, the dango are distributed to worshipers.<gallery>

=== Cultural assets ===
{{Small| (Cultural properties related to Katori Shrine, excluding independent shrines)}}

=== National Treasure ===
* Sea beast grape mirror 1 side (craft)
*: Diameter 29.6 cm, rim height 2 cm, weight 537.5 grams, made of cupronickel <ref name="Tassel"/>. Made in the Tang Dynasty, China.
*: The mirror back depicts a lion, as well as various birds, beasts, and insects, on the ground pattern of grape arabesque. The mirror's name ``sea beast'' refers to {{ill|lt=狻猊|Q757972|qid=Q757972|1=Suanni}} (sangei), which is represented by the knob at the center of the mirror's back. The fox is a mythical creature in China. In the southern storehouse of Shoso-in, there is a copper mirror that is identical to the main mirror, and although the Katori-Jingu mirror is not the same mirror made from the same mold as the mirror at Shoso-in, it is presumed that the two are related. The details of how it came to Katori Shrine are unknown <ref> "Weekly Asahi Encyclopedia Japan's National Treasure" No. 89 (Asahi Shimbun, 1998 (commentary written by Akio Kawajiri)). </ref>. Displayed in the treasure museum. Designated on March 31, 1953.

=== Important cultural property (designated by the country) ===
* Main shrine (1 attached ridge plate, 1 name plate, 3 shrimp locks), tower gate (2 buildings in total) (buildings)
*: The main shrine was designated on June 27, 1977, and the tower gate was additionally designated on December 26, 1983.
* 1 pair of Koseto yellow glazed guardian dogs (craft)
*: A pair of guardian dogs from Koseto. Ceramic. The height of the Agyo statue is 17.6 cm, and the height of the Ungyo statue is 17.9 cm. Judging from its technique and style, it is believed to have been created in the late Kamakura period or early Muromachi period.<ref name="Fusa"/> Displayed in the treasure museum. Designated on March 31, 1953. The Agata statue is the design of the 250 yen {{ill|lt=Japanese ordinary stamp|Q11505970|qid=Q11505970|lt=ordinary stamp|1=definitive stamps of Japan}} released on July 1, 1976.
* Ssangyong mirror 1 side (craft)
*: Diameter 20.5 cm, edge height 5 mm (kamaboko shape), made of white bronze. It is inscribed with the date {{ill|lt=Kyuan|Q1193860|qid=Q1193860|1=Kyūan}}5 ({{ill|lt=1149|Q19638|qid=Q19638|1=1149}}) of the Heian period, and is the oldest known example of a Japanese mirror with an inscription on the back. The style of the pattern on the back of the mirror is different from that of typical Japanese mirrors, and appears to have been influenced by the Goryeo mirrors of China's Song Dynasty or Korea. Displayed in the treasure museum. Designated on November 14, 1953.
* Katori Oune Gike Documents, 15 volumes, 7 volumes (381 letters) (ancient documents)*: An ancient document handed down by the Katori family, who inherited Ominegi. <ref name="Fusa"/> consists of 381 documents from the late Heian period to the Edo period. <ref name="Fusa"/> is considered to be a representative relic among shrine documents in the Kanto region. Privately owned. Designated on June 6, 1985.
