|}Similar to the above-mentioned Katori Naesen-kami, Kashima Naesen-kami is also located in Mutsu Province at Kashima Shrine, and eight shrines can be seen in the ``Engishiki'' divine name book. From this, it is believed that when the forces of the Yamato court moved north along the coast, they looked up to the divine power of Kashima-kami and Katori-kami {{Sfn|Kashima Migo Shrine (National History)|1983}}. In addition, {{ill|lt=Shigama Shrine|Q133753|qid=Q133753|1=Shiogama shrine}} in Ichinomiya, Mutsu Province (Miyagi Prefecture {{ill|lt=Shiogama City|Q496448|qid=Q496448|1=Shiogama}}, {{Coord|38|19|08.12|N|141|00|45.47|E|region:JP-04_ type:landmark|name=Mutsu Province Ichinomiya: Shiogama Shrine (both Takemikazuchi and Tsunetsunushi deities are enshrined)}}), where both Takemikazuchi and Tsunetsunushi deities are enshrined is also pointed out as an indication of this state of affairs.In the early stages, Kashima was said to have aimed at the Sotome (Ezo) and Katori towards the Inland Sea (Katori Sea) {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Gods)|1984}}. After that, only two Katori Naesen deities were enshrined in Kurihara County (currently around Kurihara City, Miyagi Prefecture), and they are enshrined in the north beyond Kashima, whose northernmost point is Oshika District (currently around Ishinomaki City, Miyagi Prefecture) {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Gods)|1984}} Regarding this, the time when Kurihara County became possible to rule is considered to be {{ill|lt=9th century|Q8083|qid=Q8083|1=9th century}}, and the Mononobe Sosa clan (Mononobe no Sosaji: clans related to Sosa District, Shimousa Province) served as the Mutsu Province Chinjufu Shogun from the 3rd year of Kounin ({{ill|lt=811|Q29946|qid=Q29946|1=811}}). ) There is a theory that points to a reversal of the divine power of Kashima and Katori no kami due to the success of the Mononobe Sosa clan, based on the fact that the shrine of Katori no kami caught up with Kashima no kami in 839, and the article mentions the order of ``Katori and Kashima'' {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Gods)|1984}}.In addition, in the low wetlands along the {{ill|lt=Tonegawa|Q177452|qid=Q177452|1=Tone River}} and {{ill|lt=Edogawa|Q1194505|qid=Q1194505|1=Edo River}} in the western part of the former Shimousa Province, when the land was developed after the 10th century, the Katori god was named {{jal Ink|Katori Shrine|Q1392097}}, there are many branch shrines distributed there (see "{{ill|lt=Katori Shrine|Q11667187|qid=Q11667187|1=Katori Shrines}}") {{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=40}}. In addition, {{ill|lt=Ichinomiya Nukizen Shrine|Q10863796|qid=Q10863796|1=Nukisaki Shrine}} in {{ill|lt=Ueno Province|Q1054838|qid=Q1054838|1=Kōzuke Province}}Ichinomiya, which also enshrines the main deity of Tsunetsu ({{jal ink|Gunma Prefecture|Q129499}}{{ill|lt=Tomioka City|Q873835|qid=Q873835|1=Tomioka, Gunma}}) is also pointed out.{{Sfn|Katori Short History|1995|p=41}}.

=== Katori Jinguji Temple ===
Katori Jingu once had three temples as {{ill|lt=Jinguji|Q1074971|qid=Q1074971|1=Jingū-ji}}: Kongohoji (now abandoned), Tokozan Sojiin, and Shinpukuji.{{Sfn|Katori Jingu (Heibonsha)|1996}}. Kongoho-ji Temple is located in Miyanakadai, and was the {{ill|lt=Bettoji Temple|Q11396755|qid=Q11396755|1=Bettō-ji}} of the Jingu {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. Soji-in Temple is called the Buddhist priest, {{ill|lt=Shingon sect|Q550182|qid=Q550182|1=Shingon Buddhism}}{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Chizan school|1=UNKNOWN}}{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}. Shinpukuji's mountain name is Kyotsushintokuzan, and it belongs to the {{ill|lt=Soto sect|Q749085|qid=Q749085|1=Sōtō}} (currently the Rinzai sect {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Myoshinji sect|1=UNKNOWN}}), {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}, and had 34 koku in the early modern period.{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Kadokawa)|1984}}. Of these, Kongohoji Temple was abandoned in the first year of the Meiji era {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}, and Sojiin Temple was moved from Oino to Sawara.

=== Historical evidence ===

=== About the enshrined deity and the enshrined clan ===
Regarding the origin of the shrine, there is a theory that it was founded when the Imperial Court enshrined both shrines as a base for domination of the eastern region.<ref name="Katori Heritage"/>{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Heibonsha)|1996}}, while another theory (see below) states that the original ritual existed even before that.

Furthermore, the official name of the main enshrined deity at Katori-jingu Shrine today is ``{{ill|lt=Kunetsu-nushi|Q1107286|qid=Q1107286|lt=Futunushi|1=Futsunushi}},'' but according to "Nihonshoki," Futsunushi has another name, ``Ihahinushi (Ihahi-nushi).'' Documents showing the relationship with the shrine include Ihahinushi in ``{{ill|lt=Shoku Nihon Koki|Q1041301|qid=Q1041301|1=Shoku Nihon Kōki}}'', ``{{ill|lt=Nihon Montoku Emperor's Annals|Q1052905|qid=Q1052905|1=Nihon Montoku Tennō Jitsuroku}}'', and ``{{ill|lt=Engishiki|Q1342448|qid=Q1342448|1=Engishiki}}'', and Futsunushi in ``{{ill|lt=Kogo Shui|Q531555|qid=Q531555|1=Kogo Shūi}}''. Based on these names of gods, there is the following discussion regarding the dawn of the shrine.

'''Futunushi (Ketsunushi)'''
: ``Hutu'' is said to represent the sharpness of a sword, and is said to be the name of a god representing a sword {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (National History)|1983}}. Relatedly, in the chronicles, there is a divine sword called ``{{ill|lt=Futomitama|Q11059754|qid=Q11059754|lt=Futsunomitama|1=Futsu-no-mitama}} (Futonomitama, Kararei)'', and Futsunomitama is said to have received {{ill|lt=high It is said that it was given to Kurashita|Q11668757|qid=Q11668757|1=Takakuraji}} and later enshrined at {{ill|lt=Ishigami Shrine|Q708859|qid=Q708859|1=Isonokami Jingū}} ({{ill|lt=Tenri City|Q502196|qid=Q502196|1=Tenri, Nara}}), the Ujigami of Mononobe.: The divine names of Futsunushi and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Wakafutsunushi|1=UNKNOWN}} often appear in "{{ill|lt=Izumo-no-Kuni Fudoki|Q11395858|qid=Q11395858|1=Izumo no Kuni Fudoki}}" and are said to be widely distributed in various countries. 126-129. </ref>. This is said to be because the Mononobe clan conquered various regions with the sacred sword Futsunomitama, and as a result, Futsunushi, the deified version of Futsunomitama, were enshrined in various places <ref name="Matsumae"/>. Based on these legends, it is explained that Futsunushi appears in the myth of ceding the country.<ref name="Matsumae"/> On the other hand, since Futsunushi does not appear in the "Kojiki," there is a theory that it is a feature from {{ill|qid=Q1502690|lt=Takemikazuchi|Q1502690|qid=Q1502690|1=Takemikazuchi}}, another name for "Kenfuto/Toyofuto," which appears in the "Kojiki." </ref>.
: According to the theory that the essence of the Katori deity is Futsunushi, the only difference in the description is in the Kogo Shui, which points out that this book is a book written by {{ill|lt=Hironari Saibe|Q11500712|qid=Q11500712|1=Inbe no Hironari}} criticizing the Nakatomi clan and the Fujiwara clan, and that the description is closer to the essence {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Gods)|1984}}. There is also a theory that the reason why the history books gave different information is because the origin of the ritual clan (Katori clan) was the Mononobe clan {{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Gods)|1984}}.

'''Ihainushi (Iwainushi, Ihabisu/Sainu)''': From the literal meanings of ``sai'' and ``holi'' applied to ``iwau,'' ``Ihahinushi'' is presumed to be a divine name meaning ``executor of rituals.''{{Sfn|Okada|2011}}.
: The theory that Katori no Kami is Ihahinushi is based on the fact that everything except the Kogo Shui records it as Ihahinushi {{Sfn|Okada|2011}}. There is a theory that Hironari Saibe did not have correct knowledge about the gods of the Nakatomi clan as to why only the description in "Kogo Shui" is different {{Sfn|Okada|2011}}. The names of the enshrined deities indicate a ritual structure similar to the inner and outer shrines of {{ill|lt=Ise Jingu|Q687168|qid=Q687168|1=Ise Grand Shrine}}, with ``Kashima = the god of the imperial court'' and ``Katori = local deity (servant god)''{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Gods)|1984}}{{Sfn|Okada|2011}}{{Sfn|History of Chiba Prefecture Comprehensive history of ancient times 2|2001|pp=613-628}}. It is also assumed that the reason why the shrine rank was later than that of Kashima and that there were no honors was because it was a deity to serve, {{Sfn|Katori Jingu (Gods)|1984}}, and since it was the responsibility of women to enshrine the deity, there is also a view that the enshrined deity was a goddess {{Sfn|Katori Jingu (Gods)|1984}}.As for the ritual clan, it is known that in ancient times it was the Katori clan, which called itself the descendant of Tsunetsu no Nushikami, but there is a theory that points out that the essence of the Katori clan is {{ill|lt=Mononobe clan|Q1755836|qid=Q1755836|1=Mononobe clan}}{{Sfn|Katori Shrine (Gods)|1984}}. Based on the relationship between Futsunomitama and Futsunushi, and the existence of the nearby Mononobe clan that appears in history books, it is speculated that Futsunushi was enshrined as the guardian deity of the Mononobe clan. On the other hand, there is a theory that Katori Jingu was the guardian deity of {{ill|lt=Shimokai Kunizo|Q11361123|qid=Q11361123|1=Shimotsu Unakami no Kuni Miyatsuko}}, and that the Osada no Himatsuribeuji clan, which was responsible for the country's creation, was a primitive clan {{Sfn|Okada|2011}}. The Tatadahibobe clan is religious {{ill|lt=bumin system|Q2892644|qid=Q2892644|lt=bumin|1=Bemin}}, and has a strong subordinate {{ill|lt=kabane|Q1664099|qid=Q1664099|1=Kabane}} called direct (atai), which is pointed out to be consistent with the character of the god they serve called ``Ihahinushi'' {{Sfn|Okada|2011}}. On the other hand, there is also a theory that the Katori clan was under the control of the Shimokai family {{Sfn|Matsuo|2014|pp=260-265}}.

=== Surrounding tombs ===
[[File:Matami-kofun sekishitsu.JPG|thumb|180px|right|{{Center|Matami Kofun}}]]
[[File:Shintoyama-kofun.JPG|thumb|190px|right|{{Center|keyhole-shaped tumulus of Shintoyama kofun group}}]]
The following burial mounds have been found around the shrine.
* Matami Kofun (Katori City designated historic site)
*: The tumulus that remains closest to the shrine. A {{ill|lt=horizontal stone chamber|Q11543435|qid=Q11543435|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}} has been exposed in the precincts of Matami Shrine (Kyogaisetsusha), and no burial mound remains. {{ill|lt=7th century|Q8089|qid=Q8089|1=7th century}} It is said to have been built during the Nakaha period.
* Shindoyama Tumulus Group (Shindoyama, a historic site designated by Katori City)*: A group of ancient tombs remaining north of Jingu. Consisting of one keyhole-shaped tomb and 11 round tombs, it is said to be a group of tombs dating from around the 6th century. Among these, the keyhole-shaped tumulus has a total length of 46.8 meters, and when it was first discovered in 1928, there was an argument that it was the mausoleum of the Tsunetsu deity.
*Tsumiya Tumulus Group
*: A group of ancient tombs located in the northeastern part of Mt. Shindo. <ref name="Fusa"/> consists of three keyhole-shaped tombs and one round tomb.
Although it has been pointed out that there is a relationship between these tumuli and the shrine, there are no ancient documents or legends about these tumuli left on the side of the shrine, and the details are not clear.In addition, in Omigawa, Katori City, slightly to the east, there is {{ill|lt=Sannobunme Otsukayama Tumulus|Q11354163|qid=Q11354163|1=Sannobunme Ōtsukayama Kofun}} ({{ill|lt=keyhole-shaped tumulus|Q11268718|qid=Q11268718|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}}, 123 meters), built in the middle of the 5th century, and {{ill|lt=Shiroyama Tomb No. 1, built in the middle of the 6th century. (Katori City)|Q116309884|qid=Q116309884|lt=Shiroyama Tomb No. 1|1=Joyama Tomb No.1 (Katori)}} (keyhole-shaped tumulus, 68 meters) <ref>[http://www.city.katori.lg.jp/05sightseeing/kyouiku/bunkazai/b05c.html#Vol-034 Vol-034 There are many large-scale ancient tombs, such as Shiroyama Tomb No. 1 (Katori City Home Page ``Katori Heritage''), and it is said to be the home of {{ill|lt=Shimokai Kunizo|Q11361123|qid=Q11361123|1=Shimotsu Unakami no Kuni Miyatsuko}}.
